the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms underlying the synthesis and the mode of action of syringomycins, a family of cyclic peptide antibiotics produced by the plant pathogen Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the SyrB and E gene clusters are the first examples of a novel class of peptide synthetases.
SyrB and E are the first example of a modular multienzyme complex in which the genetic organization of the modules is not colinear with the sequence of amino acids of the peptide.
syringomycins represent the first example of a peptide produced by a bacterial peptide synthetase which does not follow the “colineary rule” and which is encoded by a single transcription unit.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

syringomycins are synthesized by an unusual enzyme, syringomycin synthatase, that is encoded by a complex gene cluster and is composed of two polypeptides, SyrB and E, that bind the nine amino acids in a colinear manner, with the exception of the first two amino acids, which are bound by SyrE2.

syringomycins are produced by a single polypeptide that is encoded in a single transcription unit, and this polypeptide contains nine modules that bind nine different amino acids, and that are arranged in an order that does not respect the colinearity rule.
the syringomycins are a family of cyclic peptides produced by P. syringae and P. syringivora.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the SyrB and E gene clusters have evolved to encode a novel type of nonribosomal peptide synthetase.
syringomycins are a unique example of peptide synthetases that are not encoded by single transcription units and that are not colinear with their peptide products.

the genetic organization of peptide synthetases is much more flexible than previously thought, with the consequence that it is difficult to predict the genetic organization of a peptide synthetase on the basis of the structure of the peptide alone.
